nameStory: Polycerella emertoni is named after the "many little horns" (poly-ceras) that dot its back like tiny fingers reaching skyward. The species name honors Alpheus Hyatt Emerton, a pioneering American naturalist who studied New England's marine life in the late 1800s. While it lacks a widely-used common name, marine biologists sometimes call it Emerton's nudibranch.
description: This is a tiny sea slug called a nudibranch (pronounced "NEW-dee-brank") that crawls along underwater surfaces in New England's coastal waters. Polycerella emertoni looks like a translucent jellybean with finger-like projections called cerata sprouting from its back. These delicate creatures typically measure only 5-15 millimeters long - smaller than your pinky nail. Their bodies are usually pale or whitish with internal organs visible through their semi-transparent skin.

idTips.label: Finger-like cerata
idTips.description: Multiple slender, finger-like projections extend from the back, feeling soft and squishy like tiny water balloons when gently touched underwater

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: The body appears glass-like or milky-white, allowing you to see dark internal structures and digestive branches through the skin

idTips.label: Elongated oral tentacles
idTips.description: Two prominent tentacles extend from the head region, constantly moving and testing the water like a snail's eyestalks

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Rarely exceeds half an inch in length, often requiring close inspection or magnification to observe detailed features

idTips.label: Smooth gliding movement
idTips.description: Moves with a steady, flowing motion across surfaces, leaving no visible slime trail like terrestrial slugs do

habitat: Look for Polycerella emertoni in shallow, protected marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and among eelgrass beds. They prefer areas with good water circulation but protection from heavy wave action, often found crawling on hydroids, bryozoans, and other small colonial organisms that serve as their food. These nudibranchs are most commonly spotted in depths of 3-30 feet where their prey organisms flourish on rocks, pier pilings, and seaweed.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as water temperatures rise, making this an excellent time to spot them during low tide explorations of warming tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when reproduction occurs and individuals are most abundant. Look for them during calm weather when water visibility is best.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall, though numbers may decline as water temperatures begin to drop and some individuals complete their life cycle.
seasonality.winter: Rarely observed due to cold water temperatures and harsh conditions, though some individuals may survive in deeper, more stable waters.

funFact: Polycerella emertoni can actually steal the stinging cells from the hydroids it eats and incorporate them into the tips of its finger-like cerata for its own defense - essentially becoming armed with recycled weapons from its prey!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, pale nudibranchs, but the combination of elongated cerata, translucent body, and tiny size helps distinguish it. Remember: "Polycerella has plenty of pointy projections" - the multiple finger-like cerata are the key identifying feature that separates it from smoother sea slugs.
contextualKnowledge: The term "nudibranch" literally means "naked gills" in Latin, referring to the external breathing structures that many species in this group possess. However, Polycerella emertoni belongs to a group where the cerata serve both digestive and respiratory functions, making them multi-purpose organs rather than simple gills.
compareHints: Since no other Polycerella species are recorded in New England waters, compare with other small aeolid nudibranchs in the family Polyceridae. Polycerella emertoni differs from its relatives by having more numerous, densely-packed cerata and a more elongated body shape. The cerata arrangement is typically more regular and organized compared to the more scattered projections seen in related genera.
